title: Could future films spark revolutions or chaos by influencing people’s behavior, and what impact might this have on society in the next 20-50 years?

commenti.body:
I'm not too read up on May 68 in Paris, but from what I do know wasn't film a big intellectual medium for radical French people at the time? 

Look into the Situationists.

Film cannot literally spark revolution IMO, but art can definitely be the bleeding edge for radical activists and intellectuals that can group together to inspire or led a revolution. 

Film has certainly already been a powerful influence in shaping the world's culture though.

You'd have to accept several unpopular corollaries like media increases aggressive behaviors or that mass advertisement and propaganda is basically menticide. Broad ideas sound sexier if posed to fit the popular lexicon, but if taken to its semantic conclusion, it's pretty obvious that art is a psychological and emotional and sometimes social experience that objectively influences how we think and, consequently, how we behave. If one can only accept that art influences positive behaviors then it's hard to argue that it can also influence negative one without unleashing, vis a vis, negative behaviors.

This reminded me of a clip I saw about a VR headset for children to wear while getting vaccines. The shot is timed with a cartoon character narrating a fictional experience for kids to make the feeling of getting a shot less frightening. I could only find this clip in Portuguese: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VgCPMkNlkSI. I hope it doesn't become popular because the level of abstraction from what's really going on (needle in the arm) to a fantasy explanation is really disturbing to me. Better to educate the child about vaccines and needles and desensitize them to the pain and fear. 

The Guy Fawkes masks from V for Vendetta (comic and movie) also inspired the real-world Scientology protests and became the face of Anonymous for awhile. I'm sure there are other examples of movies that changed the world. Netflix's recent documentary, The Antisocial Network: Memes to Mayhem (2024), goes into detail about the genesis of this.

But there's a limit to how far people will go due to a movie. I've left movies inspired to do something. Unfortunately, the feeling dispersed as I walked by the concession stand into the real world outside of the theater (maybe it's just me). However, I do think VR and AR could have more impact. The movie Brainstorm (1983) explores how VR could be used to brainwash people. It scared me when I saw it on cable as a kid. A lot of Black Mirror episodes deal with this too.

I agree, media can certainly influence behavior, both positively and negatively. But do you think it could reshape our beliefs or perspectives so drastically that it fundamentally changes how we view the world?

I completely agree with your point about kids and vaccines. It’s definitely better to educate and desensitize them to the process rather than using abstraction to distract them.

I’ll definitely check out The Antisocial Network, thanks for the recommendation!

In terms of film's influence, I was thinking more about a future where directors and actors, who have mastered their craft, create movies with even more advanced imagery, VFX, and immersive storytelling. The emotional impact of these films could be so powerful that they shape the audience’s perspectives in profound ways, potentially sparking large-scale societal changes. It’s interesting to think about how far this could go in influencing collective thought and behavior.

You're right, film might not literally spark a revolution today, but as the art form continues to evolve and reach new heights, it could potentially influence audiences in ways that profoundly change their views or even unite existing movements. Even if it doesn’t lead to revolutions, how far do you think film could go in shaping and influencing society in the future?
